projectName: ACABA REDD+ Project
projectDescription: The ACABA REDD+ Project is located in the General Community Council of the Baudó River and its Tributaries (ACABA) on the Pacific coast of the department of Chocó. The Project contains very humid tropical forest with transition to tropical pluvial forest, and has unique habitat conditions for both flora and fauna. It is considered an invaluable region at the national and international level and is classified as one of the of the most biodiverse hotspots on Earth, characterized by the presence of endemic species. Significant and exponential deforestation has occurred in the region over time, which according to the IDEAM forest monitoring report for the 2010-2017 period was 10,559 ha. This scenario is the caused by a lack of territorial planning, which in turn results in processes associated with wood extraction, the expansion of the agricultural frontier, the establishment of crops for illicit use, unplanned infrastructure, the construction of new road accesses, and itinerant open-pit mining. The project uses a standalone approach and an annual average of 208,556 tCO2e are expected to be reduced with a total reduction of 6,465,226 tCO2e over the project’s lifetime of thirty years. With the implementation of the REDD+ project, the community will achieve the reduction of emissions resulting from deforestation and forest degradation, and thereby environmental and social benefits will be generated. Additionally, economic resources will be available to be invested in the creation of productive opportunities aimed at improving the living conditions of the inhabitants, in alignment with the ACABA ethno-development plan. The Project is eligible under the VCS Program and uses the VM0009, v3 Methodology. The project will have a AUDD activity type baseline scenario, using Colombia’s national Forest Reference Emissions Levels (FREL). The project will generate GHG emission reductions by reducing unplanned deforestation, covering activities within the scope of the VCS Program.

projectName: AFFORESTATION OF DEGRADED GRASSLANDS IN VICHADA, COLOMBIA
projectDescription: The grouped project aim is to recover degraded grasslands in Vichada, Colombia, through the establishment of timber plantations. The first instance consists of the afforestation of 30,605 ha of low-fertility grasslands that have been degraded by livestock in the municipalities of Puerto Carreño and La Primavera, it includes the planting of Eucalyptus (Eucalyptus pellita) and Acacia (Acacia mangium) as timber species. Through afforestation activities to recover degraded lands, the project aims to promote connectivity between ecosystems. In addition, this project is expected to provide more than 200 full-time employment opportunities (with equal access to women and men) in a zone historically affected by poverty. Furthermore, the increase in the forest cover and sequestration of carbon in living biomass will contribute to the reduction of GHG emissions by acting as sink that sequesters an average of 139,489 tCO2e per year.

projectName: ASATIQ Vaupés Maloca REDD+ Project
projectDescription: The ASATIQ Vaupés Maloca REDD+ Project is located within the area of the Association of Traditional Indigenous Authorities of Querarí (ASATIQ), which is part of the Great Eastern Indigenous Reservation of Vaupés in jurisdiction of the municipality of Mitú, in the department of Vaupés, Colombia. ASATIQ’s territory is located in the Colombian Amazon biome. The objective of the ASATIQ Vaupés Maloca REDD+ Project is to reduce greenhouse gas emissions coming mainly from deforestation and degradation of the Amazon Forest. Potential activities to reduce deforestation include forest protection and monitoring, the intensification and improvement of agricultural productivity in local communities, planting of fruit and timber trees (including those used for firewood), planting of other species used as construction materials, the creation of jobs as an alternative source of income (for example, in forest monitoring) and the improvement of health and education conditions of the communities in order to offer non-extractive work options. At the same time, actions in the medium and long terms have been defined to support the territory’s self-governance principles, as well as to promote the development of local traditional practices and ancestral education. The proposals made are framed aligned with the general action lines of the ASATIQ Life Plan. On the other hand, between 40% and 60% of recent IDEAM deforestation early warning bulletins come from the Amazon, and the department of Vaupés appears in the first five ranks of alert. Under these circumstances, the without-project scenario presents an unplanned use of forest resources with extractive logging activities and the expansion of the agricultural frontier through subsistence crops and itinerant mining, which are being developed progressively putting at risk the ecosystem balance of the forests and the cultural traditions of the communities. The duration of the project is proposed from January 1, 2018 to December 31, 2047.

projectName: ASATRIZY Vaupés Maloca REDD+ Project
projectDescription: The ASATRIZY Vaupés Maloca REDD+ Project proposed to be implemented in the Great Eastern Reservation of Vaupés is in the Reduced Emissions from Deforestation and Degradation (REDD+) category. Development of the REDD+ project is based on the VM0009 Methodology, v3 of the VCS. This methodology is applicable to this project and is being used for other REDD+ projects in the region. It has also been used by Wildlife Works, having two types of areas of application.  The first, corresponding to the Project Area (PA) and the second to the Project Accounting Area (PAA). The PAA is the area with forest cover, where the project would implement activities to prevent deforestation and whose results would be used to calculate carbon credits. According to the territory conditions, this is a standalone project that respects ASATRIZY’s autonomy. In the without-project scenario, the forest ecosystems in the department of Vaupés and in particular those in the territory of ASATRIZY are located in life zones of tropical humid forest. This area has been recognized as one of the most biodiverse in the country and the whole continent, being characterized by its endemic species. The forest monitoring carried out by the Colombian Government and coordinated by IDEAM has shown a national annual deforestation average between 177,764 ha and 219,552 ha for the 2016-2017 period, with the Amazon biome representing 70% of the total deforestation. In addition, between 40% and 60% of recent IDEAM deforestation early warning bulletins come from the Amazon, and the department of Vaupés appears in the first five ranks of alert. According to this scenario and based on data obtained from the Amazonian Scientific Research Institute (SINCHI) and through field visits carried out by WWC, it was possible to identify the unplanned use of forestry resources as the main driver of deforestation in the project area, consisting of “slash-and-burn” activities in the jungle to expand the chagras.

projectName: Bajo Atrato REDD+ Project
projectDescription: The purpose of the REDD+ Bajo Atrato project is to reduce GHG emissions from deforestation and forest degradation activities, envisioning that the efforts of the communities inhabiting and owning the territories where it is located are materialized in actions that lead to forest conservation and the improvement of living conditions. The project is located in the northwest of Colombia, in the Department of Chocó, between the municipalities of Riosucio and Carmen del Darién, in the lower basin of the Atrato River, which is part of the Darién area. In the area of the project’s first instance, the following Afro-descendant communal lands are grouped: the Quiparadó River Basin Community Council, the Curbaradó River Community Council, the Salaquí River Basin Community Council, the Cacarica River Basin Community Council, the Truandó Medio La Teresita Community Council, the Bocas de Taparal Community Council, the Dos Bocas Chintado Community Council, the La Nueva Truandó Community Council, and the Clavellino Community Council. The actions that will make possible to reduce deforestation and forest degradation in the project area are aligned with the needs and purposes  identified during the first meetings with the communities and while conducting the prior, free and informed consent process. These actions are aimed at achieving four major purposes: strengthening of governance and community management; improvement of community welfare; provision of social and community infrastructure; and boost of sustainable livelihoods and environmental protection, basic sanitation and aqueducts. The lands in the project area include tropical pluvial forests with transition to cold and very humid tropical forests. There, forests, grasslands, secondary vegetation, swampy areas and agroecosystems are found. In these areas, deforestation is associated with wood extraction, agricultural frontier expansion, illicit crop cultivation, and unplanned infrastructure construction.

projectName: Bella Bosque Vichada Afforestation Project
projectDescription: The project aims to undertake afforestation across 11,452 hectares of degraded grasslands, using a mix of native species and eucalyptus trees, and to preserve the planted areas. The objective of the project is to build biodiversity corridors across the land that is primarily dominated by cattle grazing, provide economical alternative livelihoods to local populations in the sparsely-populated region, and provide a source of material for fencing (from thinning activities, not for commercial harvesting) for local use. At the time of the project’s listing process' start (October 2024), 20.5 hectares have been planted in the Potosí farm and constitute the initial activity instance for the project. The initial instance of the grouped project is located in the Primavera municipality, roughly halfway between Puerto Carreño, the capital of the Vichada Department, which is situated on Colombia's eastern border with Venezuela, and Villavicencio, a sizable city in the westernmost part of the Meta Department. All project areas have historically been used for cattle grazing activities and rudimentary fire management practices, which have led to a continuous state of degradation, which is expected to continue. The project is expected to remove 15,374 tCO2e from the atmosphere with this initial activity instance and an average annual sequestration of 512 tCO2e. Overall, the project will have a positive community impact, providing economic opportunities to residents (and non-residents ) in the area. It will bring skilled training to seasonal and year-round employees of the project partners.

projectName: Bionersis landfill  project in Pasto, Colombia

It is an anaerobic managed landfill, owned by the municipality of Pasto and managed by Empresa Metropolitana de Aseo de Pasto (EMAS – Pasto S.A.E.S.P.). The landfill started operations in April 2001 and will close in 2034. Since its opening, the landfill has received approximately 600,000 tons of solid waste from the municipality of Pasto and neighbouring municipalities. It currently receives 220 tons of waste per day. The landfill is covered with clay and vegetal soil on areas which do not receive waste anymore. The location details of the landfill are provided in section A4. The equipment includes inter alia a gas collection network, a high temperature enclosed flare, monitoring and control systems and civil works.At a later stage, the landfill gas collected may be used as fuel for electricity generation.

projectName: BLUE CARBON PROJECT GULF OF MORROSQUILLO “VIDA MANGLAR”
projectDescription: The Blue Carbon Project Gulf of Morrosquillo is a grouped project whose expansion region includes all the mangrove forests present in the Gulf of Morrosquillo, in the Colombian Caribbean. In this region are some of the most important mangrove and marine-coastal protected areas of the Caribbean coast: the mangroves of Cispatá Bay, La Balsa-Tinajones and adjacent sectors of the Sinu River estuarine delta; the mangrove ecosystems and lagoons of La Caimanera; and the Mangrove System of the Boca de Guacamayas Sector. The main objective of the project is the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions through activities that allow the identification, prioritization and execution of actions for the adequate management of mangroves, the promotion of sustainable development, the strengthening of local governance and the promotion of alternative productive activities, while contributing to the protection of high values of community conservation and biodiversity. The Project began on May 15, 2015 and will have an expected duration of 30 years; during this period, the reduction of 1,221,717 tCO2e is expected through the implementation of activities related to four strategic lines: strengthening of governance, alternative productive projects, recovery and rehabilitation of mangrove areas, and monitoring. In addition, it is expected that this project will provide community benefits related to the strengthening of local governance and management of regionally protected marine-coastal areas, the maintenance of sustainable community management practices of mangrove forests and increased perception of the value of forest resources, as well as the economic empowerment of community groups and increased employment opportunities. Positive impacts on biodiversity include conserving the mangrove’s ecosystems and biodiversity and maintaining the hydrobiological connectivity of the coastal-marine landscape. The manatee and needle caiman are two vulnerable species that are found in this area.

projectName: Boomitra grassland Restoration in Colombia
projectDescription: This grouped project promotes sustainable grazing across Colombia’s diverse ecosystems, including the Llanos Orientales and inter-Andean valleys. Decades of overgrazing have degraded grasslands, causing soil erosion, compaction, and nutrient depletion, which reduces pasture productivity. This project supports the local ranchers in adopting practices such as rotational grazing, pasture enhancement, and improved livestock genetics suited to local conditions. Additionally, it promotes silvopastoral systems that integrate trees to boost carbon sequestration and discourage overgrazing, burning, and logging. The project will be implemented with the collaboration of field partners, who will help transfer knowledge and incentivize better ranching practices. The carbon finance resulting from this project is also expected to incentivize the implementation of the project activities. We estimate an initial yearly GHG removal of 700,000 tCO2e using the VM0042 methodology, version 2. The number of ranchers participating in the program is also projected to grow over the course of the crediting period. The project aligns with SDGs 2, 6, 8, 13, and 15, aiming for broad impact across Colombia’s grassland regions.

projectName: CARBONO VIVO- A REGENERATIVE LIVESTOCK CARBON PROJECT WITH A PARTICIPATORY APPROACH IN COLOMBIA
projectDescription: The regenerative livestock farming carbon project in Colombia is developed by the project developers Sosty S.A.S and Carbono Local+ GmbH. The project titled “Regenerative Livestock Carbon Project with a Participatory Approach in Colombia” is a comprehensive initiative developed by the project developers encompassing a variety of activities aimed at improving grazing practices, restoring soil health, and enhancing the resilience and well-being of farmers.  The primary objectives of the project are to reduce overall emissions through carbon sequestration in the soil while simultaneously improving farm productivity and conserving biodiversity in grazing areas. These goals will be achieved by enhancing livestock production practices, specifically by ceasing grassland burning and implementing adaptive multi-paddock grazing. The project will also promote the diversity of forages rather than the monoculture of pastures. This includes the management of native savannahs and introduced pastures, incorporating nitrogen-fixing species, and integrating silvo pastoral systems. The grouped project is developed within the Colombian agricultural frontier (located in five different eco-regions), which is the delimited area defined by the government, where livestock husbandry and agricultural activities are allowed to be developed. The project’s start date is 20.01.2020 and its crediting period goes on to 40 years. It targets a total 250,000 ha that can generate an annual average and total GHG emission reductions and removals of 292,050 tCO2eq per year and a total of 11,802,000 tCO2eq of emission reductions by 2060.

projectName: CHONTA COROZO REDD+
projectDescription: The CHONTA COROZO REDD+ project develops in the upper and middle basin of the Guapi river in the Colombian pacific region, known as Choco Biogeographic, characterized by its high biodiversity. This area is immersed in the territories awarded to Community Council of the Alto Guapi (INCORA Resolution 01083 of 1998). These territories have historically been characterized by the confluence of deforestation drivers, among which the following stand out: the conversion of the forest lands for crops or pastures, the extraction of elements from the forest in a little controlled way (illegal extraction of wood and extraction of firewood), population migration, illegal activities and natural phenomena promoted by human activities. By associating these phenomena with the socioeconomic conditions presented by the community council and its closets territorial environment, which is the municipality of Guapi, in Cauca. It is evident that there is a high percentage of unsatisfied basic needs, mainly related to health conditions, informal work, and education. Therefore, acknowledging these limitations for the social development of the council and the guarantee of the conservation of the ecosystems that inhabit, we bring forward the importance of generating mechanisms to strengthen local aspects to overcome these limitations. With the development of the activities framed in each line of action, it is intended to develop participatory processes that allow the establishment of a sustainable forest management system, which allows the mitigation of the threats posed by the deforestation drivers described. This through the strategy of avoiding deforestation and forest degradation through the implementation of the REDD+ project (Reduction of Emissions due to Deforestation and Forest Degradation, conservation of carbon reserves, sustainable management of forests and improvement of forest reserves in developing countries).

projectName: CO2ROZO
projectDescription: CO2rozo is a large-scale grouped project within the AFOLU sector that aims to mitigate climate change through the conservation of strategic ecosystems and the sustainable transformation of livestock systems in the Caribbean region of Colombia. Its approach integrates forest and wetland protection with the implementation of regenerative agricultural practices, combining two methodologies: VM0007 – REDD+ for the conservation of natural ecosystems, and VM0042 – Improved Agricultural Land Management, for the transition to sustainable livestock systems. The project has a 40-year crediting period, during which it plans to intervene in over 200,000 hectares distributed across private lands in the Colombian Caribbean. The project area encompasses the departments of Atlántico, Antioquia, Bolívar, Cesar, Córdoba, La Guajira, Magdalena, Norte de Santander, Santander, and Sucre, all located within the Colombian Caribbean biome—a region of high ecological value that has experienced significant degradation due to agricultural frontier expansion. This region includes critical ecosystems such as tropical dry forests, seasonal wetlands, and natural savannas. REDD+ activities (VM0007) are designed to avoid unplanned deforestation and conserve remaining patches of tropical dry forests and inland wetlands through interventions such as knowledge management, land cover monitoring, hydrological restoration, and the formalization of voluntary conservation agreements with rural landowners to protect areas of high ecological value. IALM activities (VM0042) promote a regenerative livestock model through actions such as the implementation of silvopastoral systems, elimination of fire use, and improved pasture and water management. These measures aim to restore soils, increase soil organic carbon (SOC) content, and reduce emissions associated with enteric methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O) from conventional pasture and manure management practices.

projectName: CONDOTO REDD+
projectDescription: The CONDOTO REDD+ Project seeks the conservation of forests located in the territories of the afro communities organized as the Major Community Council of Condoto and Iró, located within the municipalities of Condoto and Río Iró, in the department of Chocó. The project zone has a total area of 65.026 ha, out of which 46.191 ha were forest in 2015. The area is characterized for its high biodiversity and rain tropical forests, but also for the presence of deforestation activities and social conflicts. Deforestation drivers include mining activities, subsistence agriculture, and activities of illegal use. Social issues include absence of the state and lack of sanitation, education and health infrastructure and lack of technical guidance regarding sustainable production models. The project aims to mitigate the effects caused by climate change by reducing CO2 emissions derived from deforestation and forest degradation, restore degraded forest lands, promote sustainable management of forests and develop productive activities to improve community welfare. The project also seeks to protect biodiversity and high conservation values, enhance ecological connectivity and secure natural habitats of vulnerable species (including those within some category of threat and those that represent ecological interest.

projectName: CONSEJOS COMUNITARIOS DEL PACIFICO VALLE DEL CAUCA (CCPVC) PROGRAMA REDD+ VALLE DEL CAUCA, COLOMBIA
projectDescription: The Consejos Comunitarios del Pacífico en el Valle del Cauca REDD+ Program (called the CCPVC REDD+ Program or Program), is a grouped project which initially includes five Consejos or Community Councils located on the southwest, Pacific side, of Colombia. The initial Project Activity Instances include Consejos; Cuenca del Río Yurumanguí, Comunidad Negra Cuenca del Rio Mayorquín and Papayal, Comunidad Negra de la Cuenca del Río Raposo, Cuenca Mayor del Río Anchicaya, and Mayor de la Cuenca Media and Alta del Río Dagua. Each with legally recognized tenure over their territories, Río Yurumanguí (54,776 ha), Mayorquín and Papayal (19,060 ha), Río Raposo (20,536 ha), Mayor del Río Anchicaya (16,773 ha), and Mayor de la Cuenca Media and Alta del Río Dagua (9,423 ha). The overall Project Area (areas in which a Project Activity Instance must fall into) includes the Pacific zone of the department of Valle de Cauca in areas that are subject of unplanned deforestation and degradation (excluding any areas that have existing VCS projects registered). The Consejos in CCPVC will seek to improve livelihoods for community members and to the long-term environmental, social and financial sustainability of their territory. The location of CCPVC is near the Pacific Ocean and included major rivers that cut through the project area supporting high biodiversity. However, the territory of CCPVC experiences continuous reduction of forest cover, and the biodiversity with its ecosystems threatened. Deforestation and degradation in CCPVC has occurred due to unsustainable and illegal practices, such as illegal logging, small-scale mining, and shifting agriculture, with natural resources are being extracted unsustainably. CCPVC has directed their focus on the conservation and sustainable use of forests and other natural resources in their territories. The Project Area includes large expanses of forests and agroforestry areas that provide a crucial economic benefits to the local communities.

The project area has a total area of 1.260.222 ha at the beginning of the monitoring period. The project aims to contribute to mitigate the effects caused by climate change by reducing 27.686.867 tCO2 emissions derived from deforestation and forest degradation during the 30-year crediting period. The main activities during the Project lifetime focus in the development of productive activities compatible with community well-being and nature conservation, providing food security, improving social investment, strengthening land use planning and self-government structure, monitoring biodiversity and forest conservation. These activities aim to control and reduce the incidence of deforestation drivers such as wood extraction, mining and illegal productive activities. The area is characterized by its high biodiversity along with social unrest and deforestation. Among the activities carried out by the promoters of deforestation are moving the border of farming activities (especially subsistence agriculture and livestock), mining, wood harvesting for commercial and community use, illegal crops and colonization processes. The social problems are triggered by the absence of the government, lack of sanitation infrastructure, education, health programs and shortage of technological guidance for sustainable development. This project focuses on the AFOLU (Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Uses) sectors. Inside the category for Reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation in developing countries (REDD+). Its goal is to mitigate the effects caused by climate change through reduction of CO2 emissions from deforestation and forest degradation, restauration of degraded forest lands, promotion of the sustainable wood harvesting and carry out development activities for the community well-being.

projectName: El Estero biogas recovery and utilization
projectDescription: The El Estero Biogas Recovery and Utilization Project (hereafter referred to as the Project) is implemented by Extractora El Estero and involves the installation of a methane capture and biogas utilization system at its palm oil mill, located in Maní, Casanare Department, Colombia. The Project includes the implementation of an anaerobic digestion system and biogas collection infrastructure designed to capture methane (CH₄) emissions generated during the treatment of Palm Oil Mill Effluent (POME) in anaerobic lagoons. The captured biogas will be used for on-site electricity generation, supplying the energy demands of the palm oil processing facility. This system displaces fossil fuel-based energy consumption and contributes to the overall reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The facility is located within Extractora El Estero’s industrial complex in the municipality of Maní, Casanare, where palm oil is extracted and processed. The wastewater treatment system responsible for the methane emissions is fully integrated within the operational boundaries of the site.Under the baseline scenario, prior to project implementation, POME was treated in uncovered anaerobic lagoons without any biogas recovery system. As a result, methane generated through the anaerobic decomposition of organic matter was released directly into the atmosphere, significantly contributing to climate change due to methane’s high global warming potential. In addition to these emissions, the facility has historically relied on a diesel-based power plant for its electricity needs. Approximately 299,000 gallons of diesel are consumed annually, resulting in the production of approximately 3,531,667 kWh per year. In 2022, a biomass-powered cogeneration system was introduced to complement the plant’s energy supply; however, diesel remains the principal energy source under baseline conditions.

The energy generated is sold to the National Interconnected System of Colombia. The purpose of the project is renewable electricity generation to be supplied to Colombian power grid. The project activity considered the production of clean hydroelectric power using a flow of water. The project collects the waters of the Guadalupe River at 2,089 meters above sea level, driving the water through an open channel to the sedimentation unit. The water passes through a closed channel to a load tank, moving to a pressurized conduction penstock and a distributor, where the flow is directed to one Francis turbine. The turbine is hosted in a surface power house with their respective generator, valves and control panels. The substation is located besides the power house. As the project plant is a run-of-river hydro, a reservoir is not utilized.

projectDescription: The project “Natural silvopastoral systems in the Colombian Orinoquia Region” is a grouped project comprising a set of activities to improve grassland management. The project primary objective is to achieve a reduction in overall emissions by focusing on carbon sequestration. This will be accomplished by enhancing livestock practices through the following project activities: - Implementation of adaptive multi-paddock grazing with improved deep-rooted grass cultivars, specifically Urochloa humidicola, - Human-assisted regeneration of arbustive chaparros (Curatella americana) on paddocks to harness the potential of existing natural processes of seed dispersal and resources to restore woody vegetation, - Cease grassland burns, and - Natural regeneration of tropical, highland savannah vegetation in buffer zones around riparian forests, and environmental. The project activities will take place in approximately 150,000 ha of Vichada and Meta, two of the four departments of the Orinoquia region in Colombia, referred to here as “Colombian Orinoquia”. The crediting period is 2020 to 2040 applying the VCS Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management VM0042 Version 2.0. An estimate of the annual average and total GHG emission reductions and removals are approximately 270,000 t CO2eq per year and 5,400,000 t CO2eq, respectively. With its implementation, project instances will see an increase in livestock production, alongside overall emissions reduction driven by soil carbon sequestration. Prior to the implementation of the project, livestock practices in the regions are characterized by annual burning of savannas and low-quality animal feed. It is also expected substantial contribution to the sustainable development goals (SDGs) 2 Zero hunger, 8 Decent work and economic growth, 9 Industry, innovation and infrastructure, 12 Responsible consumption and production, 13 Climate action, 15 Life on land, and 17 Partnerships for the goals.

projectName: Origen Atrato-Baudó REDD+ Project
projectDescription: The Atrato-Baudó REDD+ Project aims to reduce GHG emissions from deforestation of natural forest. It is expected to achieve this through implementation of community actions framed in conservation, protection and sustainable management of the forest, which lead to improvements in living conditions in the territories. The area of the project’s first instance is located in the Tumbes-Chocó-Magdalena bioregion, in the municipalities of Alto Baudó, Quibdó, Lloró, Bagadó, Tadó, Río Iró (Santa Rita) and Cértegui, in the department of Chocó. The project is designed as a grouped project, initially made up of the collective territories of the following Afro-descendant communities: Community Council of San Isidro, Community Council of Villa Conto and Major Community Council of the Alto Atrato Popular Peasant Organization (COCOMOPOCA).  The project activities are aligned with the community needs and purposes identified during the process of relationship and free and informed prior consent developed with the communities. These actions are aimed at achieving four major purposes, which are: Governance and community management; social and community infrastructure; sustainable livelihoods and environmental protection, basic sanitation and aqueducts. Currently, the forests in the project area include areas of very humid tropical forest with transition to Tropical Rainforest. These ecosystem characteristics potentiate the habitat conditions of both flora and fauna, being cataloged as one of the most biodiverse areas of the country and the continent, characterized by endemism.  Deforestation that occurs in the project area are the result of a combination of complex socioeconomic and historical factors, associated with extractive processes that have directly affected biodiversity and ecosystem services. The project, as an alternative to conversion, aims to maintain carbon stocks through sustainable forest management, promoting improvements in the living conditions of local communities.

projectDescription: Project Uramia is a large-scale, community-led REDD+ initiative in Colombia’s Chocó Basin, one of the world’s most biodiverse forest regions. Located in the Bajo Atrato region (Río Sucio and Carmen del Darién, Chocó Department), the project protects 255,220 hectares of intact tropical forest across six Indigenous resguardos. Project Uramia applies a rights-based, community-centered conservation model combining active forest protection, community-based monitoring and patrols, and strengthened Indigenous governance through elected Project Councils and participatory land-use planning. The project promotes sustainable livelihoods—including non-timber forest product value chains, agroforestry, and artisanal activities—with a strong focus on women and youth, reducing reliance on destructive land-use practices. The project targets Avoided Unplanned Deforestation (AUD) under Verra VCS Methodology VM0048 v1.0, with a 40-year crediting period (May 2024–May 2064). Currently, the land use scenarios include the expansion of the cattle frontier, subsistence agriculture and illegal logging of timber species. The data does not show a trend of decreasing change or stabilization, confirming the problem of deforestation is recognized as one of the most critical environmental liabilities for the country. Based on data obtained from the Instituto Amazónico de Investigaciones Científicas SINCHI and through field visits conducted by WWC, the main driver of unplanned deforestation affecting the project area is the clearing and burning of forest for extensive cattle ranching, accompanied by the construction of unplanned road accesses. Other identified causes of deforestation are illicit crops (coca, etc.), illegal mining, and illegal timber extraction. As a result of the work with the community, activities aimed at reducing deforestation and forest degradation were identified, such as: protection and monitoring of the forest, intensification of Eco-Friendly agriculture, substitution of firewood, generating alternatives to meet the demand for construction materials, creation of jobs (Alternative Income), in addition the community is interested in strengthening the governance of the territory, as well as developing initiatives to generate wellbeing in the community associated with educational, health, cultural and sports projects.

projectName: REDD++ Manglares del Bajo Baudo
projectDescription: The Bajo Baudó Mangroves REDD++ Project is in the Pacific region in the department of Chocó, Colombia. It limits to the north with the municipality of Nuquí, to the south with the municipality of Medio Baudó, to the east with the municipality of Atrato and to the west with the Pacific Ocean. The project area is collectively owned by 5 Community Councils, which are Cuevita (R 2701/Dec 21, 2001), Pavasa (R 2695/Dec 21, 2001), Villa María de Purrichá (R 1129/May 23, 2000), Virudó (R 2698/Dec 21, 2001) and San Agustín de Terrón (R 3369/Dec 21, 2000). Although the total titled area for the 5 councils is 73,611 ha, the project area is 62,212 ha, which overlaps 51% with the DMRI Encanto de los Manglares del Bajo Baudó Management District, created through the agreement 008 of 2017. The (DRMI) is a Protected Area category that decentralizes the power of the environmental authority and allows decision-making by the communities that inhabit it. With the management of the area, new models of social and environmental territorial management have been created, however, there are several challenges in terms of governance and conservation of ecosystems. Through the DMRI declaration, sustainable management agreements have been reached with the communities and joint restoration and monitoring actions have been developed with the participation of other key institutional actors. The project area overlaps with two important ecosystems, mangrove forest (19.88% of the total project area), with an estimated average reserve of 800 tCO2e/ha, and Basal humid forest (80.12% of the total project area), with an estimated average reserve of 604 tCO2e/ha. The drivers of deforestation in the baseline have been due to the implementation of coconut crops, subsistence crops, crops for illicit use, and livestock; the drivers of degradation have been selective logging, illegal mining, fishing, and indiscriminate housing. projectName: REFORESTATION OF GRAZING LANDS HACIENDA EL MANANTIAL IN PUERTO LÓPEZ, COLOMBIA
projectDescription: The Reforestation of Grazing Lands Hacienda El Manantial project is an Afforestation, Reforestation, and Revegetation (ARR) initiative developed under the Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) Program using methodology VM0047 v1.1 and complying with VCS Standard v5.0 requirements. Although the project was originally registered under the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM), this submission represents a new and independent registration under the VCS Program, fully reassessed for eligibility, additionality, baseline, leakage, non-permanence risk, and monitoring requirements.  The project is located in Puerto López, Meta, Colombia, within the Orinoquía tropical savanna region, covering approximately 2,200 hectares of degraded pasturelands across four farms. Before implementation, the area was used for extensive cattle grazing and affected by recurrent fires, resulting in degraded soils, low vegetation cover, and limited carbon stocks. Historical analysis confirmed that the lands had remained non-forested for more than ten years, making them eligible for ARR activities.  The project establishes FSC-certified forest plantations combining exotic and native species, including Eucalyptus pellita, Acacia mangium, Pinus caribaea, Hevea brasiliensis, and selected native species. Activities include site preparation, planting, fertilization, and long-term silvicultural management adapted to local conditions.  Project implementation began in 2014. The baseline scenario assumes the continuation of degraded grazing lands with low biomass accumulation. By converting these lands into sustainably managed forests, the project is expected to remove approximately 28,069 tCO₂e annually, totaling about 1.12 million tCO₂e over a 40-year crediting period after accounting for leakage and buffer contributions.

projectName: Regenerating Colombian Coffee Ecosystems
projectDescription: Regenerating Colombian Coffee Ecosystems is a grouped afforestation and reforestation project initiated by PUR Projet in 2014 in the Colombian Northern Andean Montane Forests, where watersheds and coffee lands are severely eroded and biologically degraded.Colombia is the world’s third largest coffee producer and 95% of Colombian coffee-growing families operate on small plots of land, averaging five acres each. The Tropical Andes are one of the main coffee growing areas in Columbia and a major biodiversity hotspot, hosting 25% of the country's flora and being the richest ecoregion for birds in the country (974 bird species). However, Colombia’s Andean watersheds are threatened by uncontrolled deforestation due to rapid expansion of agriculture and cattle grazing, which strongly degrades the coffee farming conditions and the yields: low pollination, high erosion, frequent pests and diseases, low water resources. The lack of natural protection makes the farms highly vulnerable to extreme climatic events such as prolonged droughts, heavy rains, storms, landslides, etc. Besides, coffee farmers often depend on a single source of income and are highly vulnerable to market fluctuations: price volatility, demand variation, increased costs for inputs such as fertilizers, etc. Farms are not economically resilient and they are not resilient to climate change either. In this context, PUR Projet initiated an afforestation and reforestation project in Colombia in 2014, in collaboration with small-scale coffee farmers. PUR Projet is an international organization specialized in the development of ecosystems restoration and conservation projects, within agricultural supply chains like coffee and cocoa. PUR Projet also assists companies in insetting their supply chains and managing their socio-environmental commitments.

projectName: Restoration of degraded areas and reforestation in Cáceres and Cravo Norte, Colombia
projectDescription: The project envisions the reforestation of grasslands in Colombia. The grasslands show low soil carbon content because of soil degradation and/or climate-edaphic conditions. The A/R project activity proposes to reforest ~ 1,230 ha in the area of Cáceres/Antioquia and ~ 9,640 ha in Cravo Norte/Arauca. The project areas were previously exposed to extensive cattle grazing activities. In addition to cattle grazing, some parts of the Cáceres area was exposed to alluvial gold mining. The project seeks to promote sustainable management of forest resources in a manner that fosters natural regeneration. Since 2002, Asorpar Ltd. has been reforesting land with about 25 native tree species planted in different stand models that allow for natural regeneration of flown in seeds on the reforestation sites. Asorpar Ltd. puts emphasis on promoting mixed stands. This sets their approach apart from other commercial plantation forestry entities active in Colombia. The management of mixed stands is far more challenging than of monocultures. This circumstance is reinforced by the fact that little is known about several tree species planted in the project, particularly with regard to their growth performance and silvicultural management. Hence, the proposed project activity offers a unique opportunity to obtain valuable knowledge about silvicultural management practices for mixed plantation forestry and suitability of native tree species for commercial plantation forestry.

projectName: RESTORED PRODUCTIVE LANDSCAPES IN THE MAGDALENA RIVER MIDDLE BASIN IN COLOMBIA
projectDescription: The main objectives of this project are: First, to recover lands degraded by land uses related to deforestation, such as cattle ranching; through ecological restoration, agroforestry systems and assisted natural regeneration, to ensure the recovery of forests inhabited by many species of flora and fauna, including endangered species such as the brown spider monkey, the blue-billed curassow, capuchin monkey, the white-faced curassow, and the night monkey. Second, by implementing restoration corridors to reconnect wild populations within a grassland matrix to increase the flow of individuals, and therefore the genetic flow, of these populations and thus increase their resilience and probability of survival in the medium and long term. And third, to recover strategic areas that are degraded, such as the banks of rivers and other bodies of water or areas where grassland productivity is low. FPP Colombia (project proponent) is a non-profit organization promoting biodiversity research and conservation focusing on endangered primate species. FPP initiated one of Colombia's first studies and conservation programs for the brown spider monkey. FPP operates one of the longest-running research projects in Latin America, focusing on the brown spider monkey, one of the world's most endangered primates. FPP's activities have been concentrated in the Middle Magdalena River Valley, an area relatively little studied affected by human activity and part of a global biodiversity hotspot (Tumbes-Chocó-Magdalena). The Proyecto de Vida Silvestre, an initiative of Ecopetrol SA, Fondo Acción and WCS, seeks to conserve biodiversity in 3 regions of Colombia of biological and cultural importance, but which face increasing pressures that threaten natural resources. Through the articulation of these conservation initiatives, sustainability is sought through the development of a grouped carbon project which will generate income from carbon credits to achieve the objectives of ecosystem recovery

projectName: Saving Colombia's Cloud Forest
projectDescription: The tropical Andes are among the most vulnerable places on earth due to the dual impacts of climate change and human population pressures. With the intense and historic livestock activity in the area, deforestation in the valleys north and south have almost completely isolated the eastern forest. The remaining habitat is an oasis of biodiversity and one of Colombia’s many national treasures. The region also contains two important watersheds: the Río San Juan Antioquia, and Río San Juan Bravo Chocó.  These watersheds provide critical ecosystem services to communities living and working throughout the area and the forests are vital to protection of the headwaters of these important sources of fresh water to the surrounding communities. Without them, landslides, silting, and flooding threaten the health and safety of thousands of residents. As our planet’s climate systems continue to be altered, it is highly likely that some or many of the species found in cloud forests will be lost forever. The effects of climate change are already apparent here. As a result, many cloud forest species have started to migrate upslope to maintain a favorable climate. However, their routes are often blocked by a degraded and fragmented landscape caused by agriculture moving up the mountainside and penetrating deeper into the lowlands. Our goal is to create a large, protected area for endemic and threatened species to shield them from imminent threats, mitigate climate impacts, and prevent extinctions. Since 2017, we have worked closely with our local partner Fundación Colibri to create a vital connection across a narrow ridgeline. This ecological corridor will safeguard endemic and endangered wildlife and offers important protection for the headwaters of a major river, the primary source of fresh water for communities throughout the region.

projectName: Sembrando Futuro 2.0
projectDescription: The Sembrando Futuro 2.0 project aims to restore native forests across the Central and Western Andes of Colombia. Designed as a grouped ARR project, its first instance focuses on restoring 555 hectares of degraded lands in the departments of Antioquia, Caldas, and Chocó, with a long-term goal of expanding within the region. Restoration areas span diverse Andean ecosystems—including tropical humid, premontane, low montane, and montane forests—located between 80 and more than 3,100 meters in altitude. These forests have undergone extensive degradation due to agricultural expansion, cattle ranching, and land-use pressures. The project centers on the recovery of native forests, planting over 70 native species to accelerate ecological succession, improve forest structure, and strengthen connectivity between fragmented habitats. Restoration activities contribute to climate mitigation through increased carbon sequestration and enhanced ecosystem resilience. Sembrando Futuro 2.0 creates substantial community benefits by generating jobs, strengthening local technical capacity, and improving livelihoods through training and equitable carbon revenue sharing. Participating landowners formalize their commitments through 40-year Conservation Agreements, ensuring long-term forest protection, maintenance responsibilities, and sustained community engagement. The project promotes biodiversity conservation by restoring habitat within and around areas of high ecological importance and key wildlife corridors. At least eight IUCN-listed plant species are expected to benefit from reduced threats and habitat expansion. Planting began in September 2023, with the first instance planned for completion in 2025. This initial instance is expected to remove 159,280 tCO₂e over 40 years. Sembrando Futuro 2.0 represents a long-term, scalable effort to restore Andean forest ecosystems, enhance biodiversity, support rural livelihoods, and contribute to national and global climate goals.

projectName: Sustainable Agroforestry Cacao Meta, Colombia
projectDescription: Located in the department of Meta, Cabuyaro is a municipality whose surface equals to 832 kilometers square, with a population of 5,432 inhabitants, and an altitude of 151 meters above the sea level (DANE, Censo Nacional de Poblacion y Vivienda, 2018). The project is located in Guayabal, a small town in Cabuyaro composed of 204 inhabitants who mainly work the land, growing a variety of crops such as plantain, cassava, papaya, passion fruit, corn, soy, and cacao which are mainly sold in the local market of Villavicencio. This is a grouped project, the first area to be verified, consists of a total of 2,258 hectares composed of degraded pastures in majority and conservation areas, at the baseline. Of which 1,764 hectares will be established in an agroforestry system, with cacao being the perennial crop planted with other trees for shading purposes (Gliricidia sepium) and boundary purposes (windbreakers -Cariniana pyriformis). This agroforestry system has the goal of increase the soil organic carbon, as well as the aboveground and below ground biomass, and will recover the soil health and fertility through time. Other relevant agricultural practices that will be implemented are proper residue management as crop/tree materials that are periodically pruned are left in the soil for decomposition to build organic matter, processing of the cacao husks to produce organic fertilizer to be applied back in the field, as well as planting cover crops in bare soil areas, irrigation,  and planting boundary trees to prevent erosion and reduce wind damage to the cacao. The rest of the project area, 491 hectares, corresponds to other uses such as drainage channels, internal roads, and conservation areas which included native forest species, called morichales, riparian zones, and secondary forests. The total project area is divided into two properties, Espejuelos (1,258 hectares) and Primavera (1,000 hectares).

projectName: The Chocó-Darién Conservation Corridor REDD Project
projectDescription: The Chocó-Darién Conservation Corridor is the first REDD+ project to be issued credits for activities co-designed and implemented on a community-owned, collective land title. The project protects 13,465 hectares of tropical rainforest in the Darién region of northwest Colombia, one of the most biologically diverse regions on the planet. Developed by Anthrotect, the project is co-designed and managed with COCOMASUR, an Afro-Colombian community association in the municipality of Acandí that received collective title to the project area in 2005. Cattle ranching is very common in Acandí, and there are an estimated 47,000 heads of cattle in the vicinity of the project. Working together, COCOMASUR and Anthrotect have designed a strategy to stop the spread of ranching into the project area, thereby protecting Afro-Colombian livelihoods as well as the forests on which they depend.
